Guess the person

141 young adults aged 18 to 26 lay still in a scanner for six minutes doing nothing. Then they filled in a personality questionnaire and took a reasoning test. Each brain below is one of them. Can you tell a woman from a man from six minutes of nothing? An age? A worrier? Make three guesses and hit reveal to race the computer. Spoiler: one of the three is doable.

Day streak 4

Guess the person

Your job: look at 3 resting brains averaged into one map and say what kind of people they are.

141 real young adults aged 18 to 26 lay still in a scanner for six minutes doing nothing. Then they filled in a questionnaire about how much they worry. Each round you get a stack: 3 people's resting brains, averaged into one map. The 3 people are alike in one way, and you say which way. Are they all women or all men? All 18 or 19, or all 24 to 26? All worriers, or none of them? On the first two questions, under each answer sits that group's usual map, so you can spot the match by eye. On the worry question the maps are off, because they are no better than guessing there. Six rounds make one game.

You play against the computer and against the coin. The coin picks one of the two answers at random and still gets about one in two. The computer learned from 93,096 pairs of regions that rise and fall together in the other people's brains. On stacks like yours it gets women or men right 90 times in 100, the two ages 67 times in 100, and worriers 50 times in 100, which is no better than guessing. The map is your clue on the first two questions: under each answer sits that group's usual map, and a computer matching them to the stack is right 69 times in 100 on women or men and 77 on the two ages, so even a good match is a strong nudge and not a promise. On the worry question the maps do not help, and the page says so. Your first round comes with a short tour of the screen. Three free hints wait on every round.

    This part is written the way the lab writes. Skip it if you like.

    Each panel has one plain sentence on top. The numbers and the lab words come after it.

    Words you will meet here
    hubness
    How much one region rises and falls in step with all the other regions. A high number means a chatty region.
    d (Cohen's d)
    How far apart two groups are, here men and women. Bigger means more different. Near 0 means no real difference.
    n
    How many people a number is based on. Here n = 141 means all 141 people.
    r
    How well two lists of numbers line up. 1 is a perfect match, 0 is no match, minus 1 is a perfect opposite.
    AUC
    How well the computer ranks people. 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect.
    shuffle p
    How often luck alone does as well. We shuffle the labels many times and count. A small number means luck is unlikely.
    uncorrected
    Judged one region at a time, so some will pass by luck.
    corrected
    Judged against the best region among all 432 (432 of the 434 blobs were seen by the scanner), so luck rarely passes.
    ridge regression
    A simple way to learn from many numbers at once without being fooled by any single one.
    Fisher z
    A way of writing how much two regions move together so that the numbers behave well.
    z-score
    How many steps above or below the average person a number is. The notebook mostly uses Fisher z, which is a different thing.
    mean z
    The average Fisher z (see Fisher z) of one region with all the others.
    |d|
    The size of the difference between men and women, ignoring which group is higher.
    easy bar, hard bar
    The two cut-offs a region must pass: the easy bar (uncorrected) and the hard bar (corrected), both described below.
    shuffled brain
    A brain whose labels were mixed up at random, used to see what pure luck looks like.
    median
    The middle value when everyone is lined up from lowest to highest.
    rest
    Lying still with eyes open and no task.
    fastigial nuclei
    Two small lumps of cells deep in the cerebellum, not on the outer layer of the brain. The scanner grid has no cube inside them.
    whole-region
    Using every spot of a region, not only its most responsive part.
    fROI read
    The lab's stricter method: it measures only the most responsive 10 % of a region, not the whole region.
    head motion (mean FD)
    How far the head moved from one picture to the next, on average, in millimeters.
    Raven
    A reasoning puzzle test.
    neuroticism, extraversion, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness
    The five parts of a personality questionnaire. Neuroticism is how much someone worries.
    cerebellum
    The small brain under the back of the big one.
    cortical network
    A team of regions in the wrinkled outer layer of the brain that rise and fall together.
    network
    A team of regions that rise and fall together. There are eight here.
    atlas codes such as LH_Vis_6
    Region names. LH means left half, RH right half, then the network, then a running number.
    chance
    What pure guessing gets. Every question here has two answers and the game draws them half and half, so a coin gets 50 in 100.
    correlation
    The same thing as r: how well two lists of numbers line up.
    stack
    The 3 people whose resting brains the game averages into one map. The 3 are alike on the round's question.
    average person
    The mean hubness map of everybody in the study. When a stack is on screen, its people are left out of it.
    usual map
    The average hubness map of one group (the women, the men, the 18 and 19 year olds, the 24 to 26 year olds, the worriers, the rest). The people on screen are left out of their own group's average.
    match score
    The correlation (r) between two maps across the 432 regions, after the average person's map is taken out of both. 0 is no match, 1 is a perfect match and minus 1 is a perfect opposite.
    map rule
    Pick the answer whose usual map has the higher match score with the stack. A computer rule, measured on practice stacks.
    difference size
    How far apart the average woman and the average man are in one region, in units of how spread out people are. The same thing as d above.
    paper words
    The three topics that brain-imaging papers most often link to a region, from the Neurosynth database.
    Neurosynth
    A database that reads thousands of brain-imaging papers and notes which brain spots each topic word goes with.
    base rate
    How often an answer is right if you always pick the most common group. The game draws the two answers half and half, so here it is 50 in 100.
    leave-one-out
    Measuring a rule with the people on screen taken out of every average the rule uses, so a stack cannot help the rule find itself.
    age band
    A range of ages. The old page had four bands and the game now asks only about the youngest (18 or 19) and the oldest (24 to 26).
    region
    One patch of the brain, cut out by the map.
    blob
    One patch of the brain map that you can tap to see its name.
    volume
    The whole 3-D brain picture from one scan.
    connection
    One pair of regions and how much they rise and fall together.
    dot
    In the dot chart, one dot is one person.
    model
    The computer's recipe for turning a brain picture into a guess.
    toy
    A rough, simplified version used for learning, not the lab's real method.
    SomMot, DorsAttn, Vis ...
    Network names: SomMot is body and movement, DorsAttn is the focus network, Vis is seeing.
    Post
    Short for posterior, meaning toward the back.
    VIIIa
    One lobule (a small fold) of the cerebellum, the small brain under the back.
    cross-validated
    The computer is tested on people it never saw while learning.

    Read this first

    What a round is. A stack is 3 people's resting brains averaged into one hubness map, shown against the average person (the mean map of everybody else). The 3 are alike on the round's question: all women or all men, all 18 or 19 or all 24 to 26, all worriers or none. Every group's usual map is the mean map of its other people, so the stack cannot match itself. The round screen shows the two usual maps on the same color scale with no scores; the player matches by eye. The map rule a computer would use takes the average person out of the stack and out of each usual map and picks the answer with the higher correlation (r) over the 432 regions. The feedback card shows those two match scores.

    The measurements. For every person who can be in a question we drew 20 stacks of that person plus 2 others of the same group, the way the game draws them, and asked the rule and the computer. The computer averages its cross-validated guesses (made for people it never saw while learning) over the 3 people and answers by which side of the line the average falls (0 for women or men, 22 years for the two ages, 29 for the worry score). Guessing gets 50 in every column. A question shows its small maps only when the rule reaches 60.

    Why stacks. One brain gives 65 for women or men over all 141 people, 63 for the two ages over the 46 people in those bands and 50 for worry. Stacks of 3 lift the first two and leave worry at guessing, and one round type is simpler to play than two. The worry score comes from a questionnaire and six minutes of resting brain does not show it, so that question keeps its two answers, hides its small maps and says so.

    History. The game started with one brain and three calls at once: woman or man with two answers (the map rule was right 65 in 100), an age band out of four (26 in 100, where a four-sided die gets 25) and worrier or not (50 in 100). Only the woman-or-man call had a map clue. On 2026-11-06 every question became two answers with the usual maps as the picture clue, the age question kept only its youngest and oldest bands, and the round became a stack of 3, one question at a time.

    So where is the signal?

    The woman-or-man map has the largest differences, but no single region passes the strict bar. The map is a real clue on the age question with two far-apart bands (all 18 or 19 against all 24 to 26): the map rule is right 77 in 100 there, which clears the bar of 60. It is not a clue on worry: the rule is right 46 in 100, and guessing gets 50. The old four-band age question was not a clue either: the rule was right 26 in 100 on one brain.

    The answer. The computer tells women from men well in these people and is right about 4 times in 5 on one brain. Age and worry are guesses on one brain. The numbers: AUC 0.88, shuffle p 0.01 for sex. Toy warning: every number here is a whole-region average. The lab's real analyses use a stricter method called an fROI read. The model is one plain ridge regression on 93,096 connections. Every number was computed from region averages over the whole 3-D scan, not from single spots. The pictures are just pictures.
    How this was made (lab skills used)

    This panel is for the lab. It names the tools and steps we used, in the lab's own words.

    Data. The data are AOMIC PIOP1 on OpenNeuro as ds002785 (Snoek et al. 2021 in Sci Data). We used the fMRIPrep 1.4 resting-state BOLD in MNI152NLin2009cAsym with TR 0.75 s and 480 volumes. We also used participants.tsv for age and sex and the Raven score and the NEO-FFI. 141 of the first 150 subjects had a rest scan with sex and age recorded.

    Pipeline. The code is in pipelines/person/. 01_parcel_timeseries.py takes region means over Schaefer-400 plus the SUIT cerebellum. That is 432 regions on this grid: 432 of the 434 blobs on the atlas page were seen by the scanner, because the two fastigial nuclei vanish at 3 mm. The series are detrended and band-passed 0.01-0.1 Hz and cleaned with 24 motion regressors plus 5 aCompCor components plus cosine regressors in nilearn. 02_features.py computes the Pearson correlation between every pair of regions as Fisher z. "Hubness" is a region's mean z to all others. The 8 x 8 grid is the mean z between networks. 03_predict.py fits kernel ridge on the 93,096 connections with 10-fold nested cross-validation. The inner 5-fold picks the penalty and every person gets an out-of-fold guess. 100 label shuffles per target give the permutation p. The region-wise d and r maps use 1000 shuffles for the thresholds. 04_build_html.py writes this page.

    Lab skills used. The outlier skill's framewise-displacement rule is applied to the fMRIPrep confounds in steps 01 and 02. FD > 0.5 mm flags a volume and a run with > 20 % marked volumes is excluded (0 excluded). The sandbox skill's per-unit resumable worker pattern (atomic tmp-then-replace and skip finished subjects) is how step 01 ran while the download was still in progress. The shared viewer (common/) draws the fsaverage5 brain meshes and the SUIT flatmap. Nothing is measured on them.

    Caveats. The Schaefer atlas is defined in MNI152NLin6Asym and applied to NLin2009cAsym data by header. That is about 1-2 mm off. It is fine for region means and not for anything finer. Region averages are whole-atlas-region means and not subject-specific functional ROIs. This is a sketch of the connectome and not a lab-grade read. Mean head motion correlates with the targets as listed in the README. The model was not adjusted for it.

    These are real brains from OpenNeuro. The numbers come from the 3-D scans and the pretty pictures are only pictures. Hover or tap a region for its name.
